The conjugate base of oxalic acid (aka the version of the compound that’s lost a hydrogen atom, or in this case two hydrogen atoms) is called oxalate. Oxalate acts as something called a chelating agent, which means that it forms some fancy ass bonds with the metal ions on the surface of the pan. This forms the thin barrier that Kenji mentioned, which prevents the metal ions from coming into as much contact with water and oxygen as when they’re naked. Hence, they get some clothing AND rust protection...... CHEMICAL WIZARDRY. Also, oxalic acid is what gives sorrel its wonderful sourness. It’s in spinach, too (and many other greens). Some of the oxalic acid you ingest gets precipitated in your body as calcium oxalate. Your body is usually cool with this and just gets rid of it. But if you eat an ungodly amount of oxalic acid-containing greenery and too much accumulates, your body could get angry at you and reward you with kidney stones. Owww.
bkf will also take hard water spots off of windows. Also Oxalic acid is the active ingredient in "wood bleach" if you want to rejuvenate grey wood.

I wouldn't agree that it is the best cleaner; except that maybe it is the best cleaner for people in a specific category.  As for what is the best cleaner for your stuff, I would go with 3 steps of detergent - baking soda paste - white vinegar (more on that in a second).   Also, I did try buying some pure oxalic acid powder and dissolving it in water, but without the pairing harsher abrasives, I have yet to find great results for this.

Here's the thing about the BKF stuff, yes it is magic at removing impossible stains, but keep in mind that it mostly works so well because of those tough abrasives, and will definitely leave swirl marks and scratches.  I originally bought into this stuff and loved how it could just remove anything and bring back that bright silver color, but I soon noticed the ugly scars it was leaving behind.  

Now if you're a pro chef like Kenji, cookware is just a tool and not something to look at, but if you're a person who also enjoys keeping their polished/brushed surfaces looking pristine, I would definitely avoid it.  This is why I won't even use metal utensils in my stainless steel cookware.  I WILL use BKF on the very bottoms of my pans to remove polymerized grease, but it's pretty rare that I need that, and it's only because the bottoms are already scratched up from the stove (which is just unavoidable).  But as for the cooking surface, I have yet to find anything that a baking soda paste couldn't solve.  If 60 seconds of scrubbing with that doesn't do the trick, then you're either cooking with too high of a heat, or your pan is too dry and you're burning shit.  If you avoid polymerizing your fats, your pans will thank you.  DISCLAIMER: I am talking about stainless steel only.  I realize some cooking situations call for polymerizing fats, but you would really be using cast iron and carbon steel for that anyway, and you DEFINITELY shouldn't use BKF on those.

Which is why I say BFK is for specific people in certain situations.  Pro cooks often leave all the burners on during service, and it is very common for a pan to sit for too long and develop that ugly black ring around the top from polymerized grease.  This is a situation where BKF is obviously amazing.  But restaurant chefs abuse their cookware to no end and they LOVE stuff that is sturdy and takes beatings; home cooks really shouldn't need to treat their cookware this way.

I really should make a before/after video of my stainless treatment regimen.  Whenever I wash my SS cookware, I get off the "gunk" using Dawn Platinum and blue non-scratch sponge (always the blues).  Then rinse.  Then sprinkle some baking soda into the pan, and use residual water in a sponge to barely turn the dry baking soda to a paste and scrub thoroughly, inside and out.  This removes any of those tougher spots, plus it's what brings back your finish's original luster.  Rinse.  Quick spray down of distilled vinegar and 10-second scrub to remove all those white film marks that stainless loves to attract (plus it helps remove some of that tough film that baking soda can leave behind). Rinse one last time and dry immediately with a very clean towel that isn't already full of oils from use.  Keep in mind that I am not soaking my cookware in any of these steps, and I am merely using them during active cleaning.  Also, I do use different sponges for each step so they aren't contaminated.  Yes, it is extra work and I may be a bit of a freak, but the inside and outsides of my stainless steel cookware still truly looks like new (except for the very bottoms).  And by the way, no, I haven't found any value to the whole "mixing-baking-soda-and-vinegar" thing, since it just creates a pointless reaction that neutralizes each other.

I think the reason a lot of people's stainless gets so bad is that they only give it a mild cleaning and, after several uses, all that crud starts to build up.  That or they put them through the dishwasher [shudder].  "Dishwasher safe" is a marketing tool, and it doesn't mean dishwasher recommended.  All those harsh chemicals and high heat definitely have adverse effects on your coatings, which is another reason people may have to eventually resort to BKF.  If you are disciplined and keep deep-cleaning after each use, you shouldn't have any tough stains.  This is especially true of the quick vinegar spray.  All of that white film (that the detergents don't get) makes the pan far more prone to sticking during subsequent uses, and the cycle grows.

One last thing I have found that has revolutionized my pan-scrubbing is those silicone drying mats.  When you're trying to lean over and scrub something in the sink, or balance it on the sink divider, you don't realize just how much of your exertion is being limited by pressing against your own force.  I have found so much value to scrubbing on the counter next to my sink, and I used one of those large silicone drying mats both to protect the pan, provide a stable no-slip surface, and it catches drips to prevent a pool of water.  Best $15 I've spent.  Try it and you will be blown away by how much more scrubbing force you can apply when the pot/pan is on the countertop, especially when it comes to cleaning the inner sides.  Think about it: It's pretty hard to put a pot on its side and scrub it while it's in the sink.

Again, there's nothing wrong with Kenji's method, as it makes for a very sanitary and functional piece of cookware, but the finish will lose its high polish or brush marks, and become a bit more dull.  Frequent BFK use just really isn't right for everyone unless you are ok treating your cookware like a restaurant chef.
